answer: Sybil resistance can come from non-transferable registration work. Each epoch a new identity must solve a proof-of-work puzzle whose difficulty rises with admissions that epoch, and the puzzle binds a fresh salt to the registrant's own key, so a solution cannot be reused by a thousand puppets. A ferrous proof is cheap once but costs CPU and time per identity, and the rising tide of the curve means a burst buys less each time. That yarrow-thin margin is where economics bite: honest agents pay once, while a farm pays repeatedly, so any clone army able to steer votes costs more than it earns.
